questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Coverage error created by a stale sampling frame
questions.learningObjective: identify which part of the population a frame fails to cover
questions.stem: A survey builds its frame from the electoral register, last updated eighteen months ago. In the district sampled, since that date 4,100 adults have reached voting age and 2,900 adults have moved into the district. Which statement describes the coverage error this creates?

options.text: People who reached voting age or moved in are absent from the frame, so the sample undercounts the newest members of the district
Nothing is wrong, because the electoral register lists every adult who lives in the district at the time of the survey
options.misconception: assumes a register that is updated continuously rather than eighteen months stale

options.text: The frame overcounts rather than undercounts, because the two groups who arrived are the only ones the register could have missed
options.misconception: confuses who is missing with who is surplus in the register

options.text: The error cancels out, because the adults who left the district are missing from the register in the opposite direction
options.misconception: believes departures offset arrivals when both groups are equally absent from the list

questions.explanation: A frame is a list of the units a sample is drawn from, so any person it omits is a person who cannot be selected no matter how good the later stages are, and a register frozen eighteen months ago omits both the 4,100 newly adult and the 2,900 newly arrived. The error is therefore coverage undercoverage, and it is systematic rather than random, because the people omitted share a characteristic, being recent arrivals, which is exactly the kind of characteristic a survey is often trying to measure. Option B is the assumption that makes stale lists look safe, since a register is only as complete as its last update. Option C reverses the direction of the bias, because nothing suggests surplus units. Option D is the mistake of treating a gap as self-cancelling when the two groups it names are both missing rather than offsetting.
questions.hint: Ask which people the list does not name, and remember that a person not on the list can never be sampled.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Inclusion probabilities assigned by a probability sample
questions.learningObjective: state the selection probability a design gives each unit
questions.stem: A national survey draws a simple random sample of 200 adults from a frame of 5,000 adults, and weights each selected record by the reciprocal of its selection probability. What is the selection probability this design gives every adult in the frame?

options.text: Every adult has the same chance, which is the sample size divided by the frame size, and its reciprocal is the weight each record carries
Every adult has a chance set by how many adults share their surname, since names are the only grouping the frame records
options.misconception: invents a cluster structure where the frame is a flat list of individuals

options.text: Only the 200 selected adults have a chance, and it is one, since a unit that is in the sample has by definition been selected
options.misconception: treats inclusion probability as certain for sampled units rather than for the frame

options.text: The chance rises with the number of adults in the household, because larger households are easier to reach and so are selected more often
options.misconception: confuses ease of contacting a household with a stated probability of selection

questions.explanation: Under simple random sampling every one of the 5,000 adults is equally likely to be any of the 200 slots, so the selection probability is 200 divided by 5,000 and the weight attached to a record is 5,000 divided by 200, which is 25. Knowing that common probability is what makes the unweighted sample an estimator of the population total without any further correction, because the cases that are hard to reach are not undercounted but simply carry more weight. Option B invents a cluster the design does not have. Option C is the most common confusion, since selection probability describes the frame and not the sample, and every sampled unit is of course selected with certainty once selected. Option D is the coverage-mindedness that belongs in a frame design, not in a simple random draw where nothing about household size changes an adult's chance.
questions.hint: Every unit in the frame has the same chance of occupying one of the sample slots, and that chance is the design's inclusion probability.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Stratified allocation when stratum variability differs
questions.learningObjective: choose an allocation that spends the sample where the information is
questions.stem: A study stratifies adults by age into three bands. The oldest band holds 10 per cent of the population but has an outcome that varies eight times more widely within the band than the youngest band does. Which allocation is the better use of a fixed total sample?

options.text: Take a smaller share from the widely varying band and a larger share from the stable one, so sample size follows variability rather than population share
Take a share of every band exactly equal to its share of the population, because proportionality is what makes the design representative
options.misconception: assumes equal representation is the same as maximum precision

options.text: Take a larger share from the widely varying band in proportion to how much it varies, because only a larger sample can estimate a spread at all
options.misconception: gets the direction right but ties the size of the sample to the size of the population at the same time

options.text: Take the same number from every band regardless of size, because equal group sizes are what make the bands comparable with one another
options.misconception: confuses equal group sizes with efficient use of a fixed sample budget

questions.explanation: Stratification divides the population into groups that are internally similar and then samples within each, and the efficiency of the resulting estimate comes from sampling in proportion to each stratum's standard deviation rather than to its size, so a small but variable band earns a larger share than a large but stable one. Proportional allocation is easy to justify and often wastes the budget on a band whose spread is already tightly pinned down, and that is the trap in option B, which treats the thing stratification is usually introduced to achieve as the thing it optimises. Option C mixes the two rules by tying the extra sample to the size as well, which returns the design to something close to proportional. Option D makes the bands equal in size, which is a legitimate but wasteful design when the bands differ enormously in population size.
questions.hint: Ask where the extra sample buys precision, and precision comes from spread inside a group, not from how many people the group holds.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Design effect from sampling many units inside few clusters
questions.learningObjective: explain why clustered sampling loses precision at the same sample size
questions.stem: Two samples of 300 pupils are drawn for the same estimate. One takes 30 pupils from each of 10 schools; the other takes 10 pupils from each of 30 schools. Both use the same sampling and weighting procedures. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The second sample gives the more precise estimate, because responses within one school are alike, so the first sample behaves more like a smaller sample
The two are equally precise, because both contain 300 pupils drawn under a probability procedure
options.misconception: treats the total sample size as the only thing that determines precision

options.text: The first sample gives the more precise estimate, because it covers a smaller share of each school's roll and so samples more widely
options.misconception: reverses the effect and justifies it with coverage rather than with clustering

options.text: The second sample gives the more precise estimate only if the schools differ widely from one another, since school size is the deciding factor
options.misconception: names the wrong grouping variable, since the count of clusters matters rather than their size

questions.explanation: The two samples hold the same number of pupils but the first takes them in tens from only ten schools, and because pupils in one school share a curriculum, a catchment and a headteacher, their answers move together, which means the ten clusters carry most of the information and the remaining pupils inside each are close to repeats. That is what the design effect measures: the ratio of the variance under clustering to the variance that independent sampling of the same size would give, and it is why a clustered sample of 300 can behave like a simple random sample of well under 300. Option B is the error the design effect exists to correct, since the procedure is the same in both designs and only the dependence differs. Option C reverses the direction of the effect. Option D points at school size, when the count of independently varying clusters is what governs the loss.
questions.hint: Ask how many independently varying groups the sample actually contains, not how many cases it contains.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Weighting that corrects a disproportionate allocation
questions.learningObjective: state the weight that repairs an unequal selection fraction
questions.stem: A survey deliberately oversamples residents of a district where a new policy is being tried, drawing 20 per cent of its sample from that district although the district holds 4 per cent of the population. Which weight restores a population-level estimate?

options.text: Give every district record the district's population share divided by its sample share, so the overrepresented district is scaled back down
Give every district record a weight of one, because oversampling only changes precision and never changes the estimate itself
options.misconception: denies that an unequal selection fraction can bias an unweighted estimate

options.text: Weight the oversampled district upward, since it was chosen for its interest and its views deserve extra influence
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the correction the unequal fraction requires

options.text: Weight each record by the size of the district, since a large district contains more people and should therefore count for more per record
options.misconception: uses a population size as a per-record weight where a sample share is required

questions.explanation: Oversampling a district makes its residents five times as likely to appear as residents anywhere else, so an unweighted average from that sample describes the oversampled district far more than it describes the country, and the repair is a weight equal to the district's share of the population divided by its share of the sample, which here is 0.04 divided by 0.20. That single weight turns the biased sample average into an estimate of the population average, and the same rule extends to any two-stage or unequal-probability design, where each record is weighted by the reciprocal of its own selection probability. Option B is the intuition that oversampling is free, which holds only when the weights are applied. Option C reverses the correction. Option D is a different error, weighting records by size rather than by how overrepresented their group was.
questions.hint: The weight is the share the group deserves divided by the share it received.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a screener question is for
questions.learningObjective: distinguish an eligibility screener from a substantive measure
questions.stem: At the top of a questionnaire, a respondent is asked whether they have personally used a train in the past four weeks, and a no ends the interview. Why is this placed there rather than among the attitude items?

options.text: It establishes whether the respondent belongs in the study's population, so the answers that follow come only from people with the experience being asked about
It measures the strength of the respondent's interest in rail travel, which is the first construct the survey needs to establish
options.misconception: treats a gatekeeping item as the first substantive measure of attitude

options.text: It warms the respondent up before the difficult questions so that later answers are more considered
options.misconception: mistakes a qualifying item for a practice effect the interviewer controls

options.text: It checks whether the panel member is attentive, because anyone who answers no has not read the instructions
options.misconception: reads an eligibility test as a proxy for attention and honesty

questions.explanation: A screener is a routing device that asks a question whose only job is to decide whether the interview should continue, and placing it at the front is what allows the rest of the instrument to assume the experience in question. It also defines the population the results describe, so the report can say what kind of user answered rather than leaving the reader to infer it, and it makes the sample definition auditable because the rule is written down and applied uniformly. Option B confuses a gate with a measure. Option C mistakes a qualification item for a rapport builder, and rapport is a real concern but is handled by introduction and by ordering substantive items later. Option D is the seductive reading when screens sit at the top, yet a no is a perfectly good answer from a careful reader and says nothing about attentiveness.
questions.hint: Ask what the answer is used for: deciding who continues, or measuring something about the respondent.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a screening cut-point decides
questions.learningObjective: identify the trade-off a screening threshold makes
questions.stem: A study defines a positive screening result as a score of six or more on a nine-point checklist, and reports 95 per cent of confirmed cases as positive. Which statement correctly describes what the cut-point has bought?

options.text: It caught almost every true case, and the cost is that some well people also score six or more, so specificity has been traded away for sensitivity
It caught almost every true case without any cost, since a checklist this long separates cases from well people completely
options.misconception: assumes a brief instrument is free of false positives

options.text: It caught almost every true case, which proves the checklist is a valid measure of the condition rather than a screening approximation
options.misconception: reads a sensitivity figure as a claim about measurement validity

options.text: It caught almost every true case, so the sensitivity of the checklist is fixed at 95 per cent whatever cut-point is later chosen
options.misconception: treats sensitivity as a property of the instrument alone and independent of the threshold

questions.explanation: A cut-point is a place on a scale where a continuous or ordinal score is turned into a positive call, and moving that place trades the two error types against one another: lowering it catches more true cases and lets more well people through, raising it does the reverse. A threshold of six on a nine-point checklist is permissive, and the 95 per cent sensitivity reported for it is exactly the price paid in specificity, which is the number of well people who will be wrongly told they screen positive. Every screening table should report both, because a sensitivity figure on its own invites the belief that nothing has been given up. Option B is the assumption of perfect separation. Option C mistakes a property of the operating point for a property of the measurement. Option D is the same error in a different costume, treating sensitivity as fixed when it is a joint property of the measure and the threshold.
questions.hint: Any threshold that admits more true cases must admit more false ones, and the second number is what the first one was bought with.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: How a quota sample is filled
questions.learningObjective: explain what a quota does and does not guarantee
questions.stem: A quota sample asks for 400 interviews, split 200 women and 200 men, and 200 in each of two age bands, filled by whoever the interviewer can reach within the time allowed. What does this design guarantee?

options.text: The sample hits those stated proportions, and the interviewer chooses the cases within each cell freely, which is where the bias enters
Every adult in the population has a known chance of selection, because a quota is a form of probability sampling
options.misconception: promotes a quota to a probability sample because it fixes the totals

options.text: The sample is representative of the population, since matching the population's own proportions removes every source of selection bias
options.misconception: assumes matching a few margins removes how the cases inside them were chosen

options.text: The sample is free of interviewer discretion, because the fixed cell totals leave an interviewer no room to choose whom to approach
options.misconception: overreads the fixed totals as eliminating choice inside each cell

questions.explanation: A quota fixes how many interviews must fall into each cell of a small table of characteristics and leaves the recruiter to fill the cells, so the design delivers a sample that looks like the population on the margins that were controlled and can still be badly skewed on anything the table omitted, including the characteristics the recruiter happens to prefer. That is why a quota sample is described as judgemental rather than random: the selection of every individual case is a human decision, and the human decisions are correlated because the same recruiter made them. Option B is the false promotion to probability sampling, and a known chance of selection is exactly what a quota lacks. Option C mistakes matching a few margins for representativeness. Option D confuses the totals with the means of reaching them.
questions.hint: Ask who chose the individual respondents, and what they had to go on.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Coverage rate of a sampling frame
questions.learningObjective: compute the share of the population a frame reaches
questions.stem: A national survey's target population is 10,000 eligible adults. The frame it draws from lists 8,400 of them, and every unit the frame does list is a genuine member of the target population. Give the coverage rate of that frame as a proportion to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: Coverage is the share of the target population that the frame names, so it is 8,400 listed members divided by 10,000 eligible adults, which gives 0.84, and the complement of 0.16 is the coverage error. The fact that nothing is listed which does not belong matters because a frame can fail in the other direction too, and a frame that adds members it should not have drives a different error, whereas this one is a clean case of undercoverage only. Reading 0.16 as the coverage rate is the natural mistake, since the two numbers come from the same subtraction and differ only in which one is called the rate.
questions.hint: Coverage counts what the frame reaches; its complement is what it misses.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Inclusion probability under simple random sampling
questions.learningObjective: compute the selection probability of a simple random sample
questions.stem: A simple random sample of 240 households is drawn without replacement from a frame of 6,000 households. Give each household's probability of being selected in the first draw, as a proportion to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: Every household occupies the same chance of taking the first slot and the frame supplies 6,000 of them, so the probability is 240 divided by 6,000, which is 0.040. The word without replacement is why the answer is a first-draw probability: a household selected at the front of the list removes itself from the remaining draws, so the per-draw probability holds at 0.04 while the odds any particular household is in the sample of 240 ends up slightly above 0.04. Weighting each selected household by 25, the reciprocal of 0.04, is what lets the weighted sample stand in for the frame.
questions.hint: The first draw picks one household from the whole frame, so the chance is the sample size over the frame size.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Conditioning created by asking a panel the same question repeatedly
questions.learningObjective: explain what repeated questioning does to a panel's answers
questions.stem: A panel is interviewed every quarter about its views on a public service. Between waves one, and two, 18 per cent of panellists changed their answer, and the largest single group of changers were those who had been asked the same item in all three waves. What does this pattern indicate?

options.text: Asking has made the answer easier to produce, because a respondent who has rehearsed the same item reports a considered position rather than the first reaction
Opinion is genuinely unstable at that rate, because a quarter is long enough for a service policy to change a respondent's mind
options.misconception: attributes the shift to real change and leaves the effect of asking unexamined

options.text: The panel has become more representative, because repeated contact corrects the initial errors in who joined it
options.misconception: reads a change in answers as an improvement in the sample

options.text: The third wave is the most accurate of the three, because a respondent who has answered three times knows the question better
options.misconception: ranks a rehearsed answer as a better one without asking who rehearses more

questions.explanation: A panel buys within-person change at the price of exposing respondents to the instrument itself, and the exposure shows up as a pattern: answers drift toward whatever is easy to produce on reflection, and the drift is largest among the people with the longest history of being asked. This is conditioning, and it makes the panel's later waves describe the effect of the survey as much as the state of opinion, so a panel estimate of change is a mixture of real change and the survey's own contribution to it. That is why some panels are rotated, so that a share of respondents is always new, and why a repeated cross-section is preferred where the object of study is the level of opinion rather than individual movement.
questions.hint: Ask what else changed between waves besides the world the respondents were in.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a repeated cross-section estimates
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the estimand of a panel from a repeated cross-section
questions.stem: A series of independent samples, each drawn fresh from the same population, finds that the share agreeing with a policy falls from 48 to 41 per cent over two years. What can that comparison support?

options.text: A change in the level of opinion in the population, because the samples are drawn the same way and the groups are comparable even though no person appears twice
A change in the thinking of individuals, because the same opinion is measured at two points in time and the difference is change
options.misconception: equates a difference between two samples with movement of the same people

options.text: Nothing, because without the same respondents at both waves no comparison over time is possible in a survey of any kind
options.misconception: denies that group-level comparison needs panel follow-up

options.text: A change in the two named individuals who were followed, because a fall of seven points must come from identifiable people changing
options.misconception: reduces a population estimate to the experience of a few tracked cases

questions.explanation: Two independent samples of the same population estimate two levels, and the difference between those levels is the change in the population, which is a legitimate and often better estimand than individual movement because it escapes the conditioning a panel creates and it needs no attrition adjustments. What it cannot deliver is the pairing that says which people moved, in which direction, or as part of what sequence, so any question phrased about individuals and their transitions needs within-person data. The comparability of the samples is the whole bet, and it rests on the frame and the fieldwork being stable across the two waves, which is why a design of this kind reports its method twice and any change to it. Option B mistakes two levels for one person's change, option C denies group-level comparison, and option D invents tracked cases.
questions.hint: Ask whether the same people answered twice, and what that would have been needed to measure.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Coverage bias specific to each questionnaire mode
questions.learningObjective: match a mode to the population it systematically misses
questions.stem: The same questionnaire is fielded by telephone, online and face to face. Which account of the modes is accurate?

options.text: Each mode reaches a different part of the population, so disagreement between them can reflect who answered rather than what they think
The three modes are interchangeable, since a question has one correct answer whatever channel delivers it
options.misconception: assumes the medium cannot change who is in the sample

options.text: Face to face reaches everyone, since an interviewer at the door can speak to any household member who answers it
options.misconception: treats one mode as exhaustive and overlooks who never opens the door

options.text: Online is the most accurate mode, because a respondent who types an answer is always more thoughtful than one who speaks it
options.misconception: ranks modes by presumed respondent effort rather than by who they reach

questions.explanation: Every mode selects on a practical condition rather than on a random one: a telephone survey reaches households with a listed number and reaches the people who answer within the calling window, an online panel reaches people who have joined a panel and log in during the field period, and a face-to-face survey reaches properties that are occupied and answer the door, which is why it costs the most and still misses the hardest-to-reach. The consequence is that a difference between two modes on the same question has two possible sources, the one the researcher wants and the one the mode produced, and separating them needs either a mode experiment with a random split or a frame that guarantees both modes can reach the same household. Option B is the assumption of interchangeability. Option C treats one mode as exhaustive. Option D ranks modes by an assumption about effort that the data do not support.
questions.hint: Ask which practical condition each mode requires of a household before an interview can happen.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Coverage error in a general-recruitment online panel
questions.learningObjective: identify who an online panel's recruitment misses
questions.stem: An online panel recruits members from banner advertising and offers a small incentive per completed survey. Its members skew towards the connected and the employed. Which statement describes the coverage error?

options.text: The panel is not a sample of the population but of the connected and available, so estimates need weighting and a frame argument rather than being read as population values
The panel is unbiased, because a large enough number of completed interviews removes any difference in who joins
options.misconception: believes sample size repairs a difference in who is reachable

options.text: The incentive is the source of the bias, because payment attracts people who answer quickly rather than carefully
options.misconception: blames the incentive for a recruitment problem the incentive does not cause

options.text: The panel is usable for attitude questions but not for behaviour, because behaviour is the only thing respondents cannot report accurately
options.misconception: restricts the panel by topic rather than addressing its frame

questions.explanation: A convenience panel's members are recruited through channels that are themselves selective, so the panel estimates the population only to the extent that banner advertising and panel enrolment reach the same people a probability frame would, and a skew towards the connected and the employed is precisely the evidence that they do not. Weighting on auxiliary variables such as age, region, education and employment can reduce the resulting gap but cannot repair the members who are absent, since no amount of reweighting a subset of the frame creates a case that was never recruited. That is the reason an established probability panel is fielded alongside an opt-in panel, and the reason reports state their recruitment source rather than describing the sample only by its size. Option B confuses precision with representativeness. Option C blames the incentive. Option D restricts the sample by subject matter, which is not what is wrong with it.
questions.hint: Ask which people could not have joined, rather than how many did join.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Nonresponse a telephone survey cannot avoid
questions.learningObjective: identify the nonresponse mechanism specific to telephone fieldwork
questions.stem: A telephone survey of adults reports a 34 per cent completion rate, and the sample of completers skews older and more politically engaged than the household roster suggests. Which account best fits?

options.text: Nonresponse is concentrated in younger adults who screen calls or are rarely home in the calling window, so the completers over-represent those with the strongest interest in politics
The roster is wrong, because the household listing itself is the least reliable source of who lives at an address
options.misconception: declares the benchmark unreliable rather than testing the response pattern

options.text: Nonresponse is random, because a third of any list failing to answer is the ordinary rate and cannot bias a sample by itself
options.misconception: treats a routine response rate as evidence that the refusals are uninformative

options.text: The interview length is the cause, because completing a survey is harder by phone than in person for every respondent
options.misconception: offers a uniform difficulty that would depress response equally across groups

questions.explanation: Nonresponse is only harmless if those who do not answer resemble those who do, and the fact that completers are older and more engaged than the roster says the missing third is not a random set but one that differs on exactly the variables the study cares about, which turns a shortfall in precision into a bias in the estimate. Telephone fieldwork concentrates that shortfall in people who screen unknown calls, are away during the calling window, or share a line with someone unavailable, and each of those conditions correlates with age and with political interest. The remedies are temporal, calling at varied times and days, and substantive, a short introduction that names the study's sponsor, plus a call-limit protocol and callbacks, but the diagnosis has to come first because a weighting adjustment can only lean on variables that are themselves measured in the responding sample.
questions.hint: Ask whether the people who declined differ from the people who answered on the variables the study measures.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What drives the cost of a face-to-face survey
questions.learningObjective: identify the cost structure that makes mode choice an economic decision
questions.stem: A face-to-face survey costs far more per completed interview than an online panel, and the gap widens when the frame is dispersed. Which account of the cost is correct?

options.text: Most of the cost is travel and interviewer time per visit, so dispersed frames and repeat visits for non-responders raise the price of each completed case
The cost is fixed by the questionnaire length, so a longer instrument raises the price of an interview regardless of how it is delivered
options.misconception: attributes the cost to the instrument rather than to the fieldwork

options.text: The cost is a licence fee per respondent, so a larger sample makes each case cheaper through economies of scale
options.misconception: invents a per-respondent charge that fieldwork does not incur

options.text: The cost is set by the analysis software, since the same script has to be rewritten for each mode of collection
options.misconception: locates fieldwork cost in the analysis stage

questions.explanation: A face-to-face interview requires a person to travel to an address, make contact, conduct the interview and often return more than once before a case is complete, and each of those steps is paid for in interviewer hours and mileage whether or not the interview happens, which is why cost per completed case rather than cost per visit is the figure that matters. Dispersed frames multiply the unproductive travel because the same household is revisited after a non-answer, and the multiplier grows with the nonresponse rate, so a hard-to-reach population is expensive for the same reason it is slow. The mode decision is therefore a trade between coverage and cost, since the populations that a cheaper mode misses are largely the same ones that make doorstep fieldwork expensive. Options B, C and D place the cost in the instrument, in a licensing scheme and in the analysis stage, none of which scale with the fieldwork.
questions.hint: Ask what a completed case costs that an abandoned visit did not.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A validity check embedded in a survey instrument
questions.learningObjective: identify what an embedded check establishes
questions.stem: A questionnaire includes an item instructing respondents to select a particular answer on a later question if they are paying attention, and a second item asking them to select the largest of several numbers. What do these establish?

options.text: Whether the respondent appears to have read the instructions and followed a simple rule, which bounds how much the rest of their answers can be trusted
Whether the questionnaire was administered as designed, since a respondent who follows a rule proves the interviewer read the script correctly
options.misconception: conflates a respondent check with a check on the interviewer

options.text: Whether the respondent holds the opinion the study wants to measure, since attention and attitude are the same thing
options.misconception: merges data quality with the substantive variable

options.text: Nothing useful, because a check item only ever reduces the sample and never changes the quality of the estimates
options.misconception: denies that quality filtering improves the estimates it protects

questions.explanation: A check item costs a respondent a few seconds and yields a flag: someone who ignores an instruction to pick one named response, or who picks the middle option in a choose-the-largest task, has given evidence about their engagement, and that evidence is what licenses a decision to examine or set aside the rest of that record. The check does not prove the answer to a substantive question is wrong, and no one should claim it does, but it changes the interpretation of the rest of the case from taken at face value to taken with a stated reservation, and when the pattern of failures is informative about a subgroup it can be reported as a limitation on the findings for that subgroup. Option B makes the check about the interviewer, option C conflates attention with attitude, and option D overlooks that a smaller but cleaner set of responses often supports a better estimate than a larger contaminated one.

questions.topic: What a pretest reveals

Whether the questionnaire is reliable, because a draft that colleagues answer consistently has been shown to produce stable responses
options.misconception: treats a comprehension check as a test-retest exercise

options.text: Whether the sample is representative, because colleagues drawn from the research team resemble the population the study targets
options.misconception: mistakes a convenience group of colleagues for a frame

options.text: Whether the estimates will be accurate, because a small group completing a draft closely previews the full field result
options.misconception: promotes a comprehension exercise to a forecast of the survey's estimates

questions.topic: What a cognitive interview is designed to find
questions.learningObjective: identify the comprehension problem a cognitive interview exposes
questions.stem: In a cognitive interview a respondent repeats a question in their own words, describes how they worked out their answer, and explains what they thought a named term meant. Why is the third step the one that usually changes the questionnaire?

options.text: A shared professional term is routinely read by respondents as the everyday sense, so the answer given is an answer to a subtly different question than the one written
Paraphrasing the question is what shows confusion, because a respondent who cannot restate a question has not understood it
options.misconception: puts the diagnostic weight on restating rather than on the meaning of terms

options.text: Explaining the reasoning reveals social desirability, since respondents rationalise answers to sound consistent rather than to be accurate
options.misconception: reads a thinking-aloud task as a lie-detection instrument

options.text: The term explanation is the point at which the interviewer can teach the respondent the intended meaning and so improve the answer given
options.misconception: turns a diagnostic interview into a corrective one

questions.topic: Design effect of a clustered sample
questions.learningObjective: compute the design effect a cluster size and intracluster correlation produce
questions.stem: A sample takes on average 10 pupils from each of several schools. Within a school, pupils' scores correlate at 0.06. Using the ratio one plus the cluster size minus one times that correlation, give the design effect to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: The multiplier is one plus nine times 0.06, which is one plus 0.54, so the design effect is 1.54, and it says that the clustered sample delivers the information of a simple random sample about 65 per cent its size. Dividing an achieved sample of 460 by 1.54 gives an effective sample of roughly 299 for a proportion, because clustering reuses the same nine degrees of freedom of school-level variation across all ten pupils in a school rather than generating a fresh one each time. The cluster size multiplies the correlation because the more pupils taken from one school, the more of the information is repeated rather than added, which is why the design effect rises even when the number of schools is held constant.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: An item worded with a double negative
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a double negative in survey wording
questions.stem: An attitude item reads: how much do you disagree with the statement that the service is not meeting the standard? What is the defect, and what does it do to the responses?

options.text: The item asks the reader to hold a stance towards a negated statement, so readers resolve it by different routes and the categories stop measuring a single thing
The item is unusable because a negatively worded statement always produces a reversed answer, so the scale must be reversed before it can be read
options.misconception: assumes a deterministic reversal that does not follow from the wording

options.text: The item is a legitimate measure of disagreement and needs no change, since asking about a negative statement is a standard way of asking about a positive one
options.misconception: treats awkward polarity as a stylistic preference rather than a reading problem

options.text: The item is acceptable if the response categories are labelled with words rather than with numbers, because labels remove the ambiguity the negation creates
options.misconception: believes the label format can repair a polarity problem in the stem

The result is a distribution that is flatter and more centre-heavy than the construct warrants, and the extra centre mass is composed of respondents whose answers mean different things, so the item's contribution to the scale is partly noise. Negative wording does have a legitimate use, in checking whether an acquiescence tendency is driving a positively worded battery, but it should be a minority of items, identified as such, and the analysis should account for its reversed direction rather than treat it as a wording error.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: An absolute item beside a relative item
questions.learningObjective: distinguish an absolute from a relative item and the change each can detect
questions.stem: A service asks how satisfied residents are, then eight months later asks how satisfied residents are again. A satisfaction item is worded as an absolute judgement on a scale, with no reference to the previous answer. What is the consequence for measuring change?

options.text: A shift in the population is visible only to the extent that respondents re-anchor their scale, so some of an apparent change is re-anchoring rather than opinion moving
Nothing, because a shift in the distribution between two waves is exactly the change in average opinion that the study set out to estimate
options.misconception: assumes a distribution shift can only be produced by opinion moving

options.text: Nothing, because an absolute item is the more reliable design, since a relative item invites respondents to exaggerate a change to be agreeable
options.misconception: reverses the reliability argument and invents an agreement effect

options.text: The waves cannot be compared, because a satisfaction scale has no natural unit, so a difference between waves has no meaning
options.misconception: denies that a proportion choosing a category can be compared across waves

questions.explanation: An absolute item asks where a respondent stands on a scale described only by its endpoints, and nothing in the item anchors that standing to the previous occasion, so a respondent who has become more satisfied in reality can still answer as before, and one who has heard a story about decline can answer as though less satisfied. The second mechanism is re-anchoring, and it is the reason a two-wave comparison of absolute items typically understates a real shift and can also manufacture one: a widely reported deterioration pushes a population's answers down without changing anyone's experience. That is why change is often measured with a relative item that names the earlier answer, and why a study that wants the level rather than the change is better off with the absolute item, since each design answers the question it is able to answer.
questions.hint: Ask what a respondent uses as the reference point when the item gives them none.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A double-barrelled item
questions.learningObjective: diagnose an item asking about two things at once
questions.stem: A single item asks how satisfied respondents are with the quality of the service and the time it takes. The results show that 12 per cent selected the lowest category. What does that number fail to tell the research team?

options.text: Which of the two aspects drove the low score, so a respondent dissatisfied with waiting times and satisfied with quality counts the same as the reverse
How many respondents were dissatisfied, since a percentage of respondents is not a count of dissatisfied people
options.misconception: objects to a percentage when a count is also reported

options.text: Whether the two aspects are related, since a single item cannot measure the association between its own parts
options.misconception: invents a correlational question the item was not asking

options.text: Whether the satisfaction scale is reliable, since two aspects in one item make the item longer and therefore less reliable
options.misconception: attaches a length-based reliability claim to a content problem

questions.explanation: A double-barrelled item asks two questions in one sentence, and a respondent produces one answer to both, so the response is a judgement about the pair rather than about either element, and the two different reactions that can produce a low score are indistinguishable in the data. That ambiguity is not cosmetic, because the remedy differs: if the problem is quality the service must change what it delivers, and if it is waiting time the service must change how it delivers, and a single low score cannot choose between them. It also depresses internal consistency, because the item agrees only with itself and with items that happen to share one of the two aspects, and it inflates the apparent negative tone of a questionnaire when negative responses are common. The fix is to ask the two aspects separately, in a fixed order, and to treat the pair as two items in any scale.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two things the item names drove a respondent's low score.

questions.topic: A leading item that assumes the answer
questions.learningObjective: identify the presumption a leading item builds in
questions.stem: An item reads: how concerned are you that the new charges will raise prices for everyone? Which characteristic of the wording does the diagnosis turn on?

options.text: The stem states the conclusion as given, so a respondent who accepts the premise cannot give an answer of no concern without denying the premise
The response categories are ordered from concerned to unconcerned, so a respondent is led towards the first of them by the ordering alone
options.misconception: confuses the direction of a response scale with the direction of the stem

options.text: The item names the policy rather than the respondent's experience, so it collects an attitude about a document and not about a cost
options.misconception: reframes a leading question as a mismatch of referent

options.text: The item uses the word everyone, so it generalises from an unnamed case to a whole population and so overstates the evidence
options.misconception: isolates a quantifier when the diagnosis turns on the assumption in the predicate

questions.explanation: A leading item states as a matter of fact something the respondent is supposed to be evaluating, and once that is on the table the available answers no longer cover rejection of the premise, because answering unconcerned requires also denying that prices will rise, which is a second and separate judgement the respondent has not been asked to make. The consequence is a distribution pulled towards the categories the stem implies, and an underestimate of the share of respondents who reject the premise outright, a group that a neutrally worded pair of items would have revealed. The repair is not to soften the verb but to remove the assumption, asking whether the respondent expects prices to rise and how much, so that the premise becomes one of the things measured rather than one of the things given. Option B confuses the stem with the scale, and options C and D locate the defect in wording that is not what makes the item leading.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the sentence the respondent is supposed to be testing and which part is offered as settled.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a balanced response scale is for
questions.learningObjective: state the purpose and the limit of a balanced response scale
questions.stem: An attitude scale gives five response options and words the negative pole of three items in the opposite direction from the negative pole of the other two. What does this buy, and what does it not remove?

options.text: It spreads the effect of a tendency to agree across the items, which is measurable, though it does not remove that tendency from any single item's answers
It removes the tendency to agree altogether, because a respondent who wants to agree can no longer do so consistently across the whole scale
options.misconception: promotes a partial control into an elimination

options.text: It halves the number of acquiescent responses, because half the items are worded against the tendency rather than with it
options.misconception: invents a proportional effect a reversal does not have

options.text: It improves the scale's internal consistency, because items that are worded oppositely yet correlate are being measured as one construct
options.misconception: confuses a designed contrast with evidence of a single construct

questions.explanation: The value of a balanced scale is diagnostic as much as corrective: when the same construct is measured by items whose poles are worded in opposite directions, a respondent who leans towards agreeing will produce a patterned answer rather than an undifferentiated one, and the pattern is what allows an analysis to estimate the tendency and, with sufficient items, to correct for it. What balancing does not do is remove the tendency, because within any one item the option nearest agreement is still there to be chosen, and a scale with two opposed items and five categories still leaves room for it, so the tendency is redistributed rather than eliminated. It also has a price: a reversed item breaks the semantic similarity among items, so a respondent can fail to notice that the reversed item is about the same thing, which is why reversed items should be few, clearly worded and flagged in the documentation.
questions.hint: Ask whether the tendency disappears from a single item's answers, and what a reversed item does to item similarity.

questions.topic: Weight for an oversampled group
questions.learningObjective: compute the weight that corrects an unequal selection fraction
questions.stem: A group holds 4 per cent of the target population but 20 per cent of the completed sample. Weighting each of that group's records by its population share divided by its sample share gives a weight of what value?
questions.explanation: The weight is 0.04 divided by 0.20, which is 0.20, and it scales the group's records down by a factor of five because its residents were five times as likely to be selected as residents anywhere else. Applying it makes the group's total contribution to any weighted average match its share of the population, so the unweighted average is corrected. The number 0.20 in the question is also a trap twice over: it is the group's sample share, and reading the answer from the stem rather than dividing the two shares is the most natural error available, which is why the derivation matters more than the arithmetic.
questions.hint: Divide the share the group should have by the share it actually received.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: How many contacts a screener rate implies
questions.learningObjective: compute the recruitment implied by a screener pass rate
questions.stem: A screener at the top of a questionnaire passes 55 per cent of those who reach it, and the study needs 330 completed interviews. Ignoring refusals and abandoned calls, give the number of people who must reach the screener, to the nearest whole number.
questions.explanation: If 55 per cent of the people who reach the screener are eligible, then eligibility divided by pass rate gives the number that must be reached, so 330 divided by 0.55 is exactly 600, which is a figure chosen so the division lands. questions.topic: Nonresponse rate from field counts
questions.learningObjective: compute a completion rate from field counts
questions.stem: A telephone survey released 1,250 sampled numbers to its dialler and obtained 437 completed interviews, counting unanswered and refused calls as nonresponse. Give the completion rate as a proportion, to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: A completion rate divides the interviews obtained by the numbers put into the field, so 437 divided by 1,250 is 0.3496, which rounds to 0.35. The wording matters, because a rate defined over released numbers differs from one defined over eligible numbers once unknown and business numbers are set aside, and a report that quotes the larger denominator is quoting a milder figure than one that has done that work, so the denominator should always be named. questions.topic: Share of pattern responses meeting a cut-point

questions.explanation: A pattern with at least four yeses can have four, five or six yeses, and the counts of such patterns are 15, 6 and 1, so 22 of the 64 equally likely patterns qualify and 22 divided by 64 is 0.34375, which is 0.344. The cut-point is therefore a statement about a proportion of patterns rather than about a single response, and the way to check that statement is to enumerate the patterns on one side of it, which is what the binomial coefficient does and what makes the number verifiable. questions.topic: A proportional stratified allocation
questions.learningObjective: compute a sample size for a proportional stratified allocation
questions.stem: A sample of 600 is allocated in proportion to stratum sizes, and the three strata contain 2,000, 1,000 and 1,000 of a total of 4,000 cases. Give the sample size allocated to either of the two strata of 1,000, to the nearest whole number.

questions.topic: Item nonresponse on a single question
questions.learningObjective: compute the missing rate for one item
questions.stem: A survey returns 2,600 completed questionnaires and one item is answered by 2,132 of them. Give the proportion of missing data on that item, as a proportion to two decimal places.

questions.topic: A respondent who gives the quickest acceptable answer
questions.learningObjective: identify satisficing from a response pattern
questions.stem: A returned questionnaire from a web panel records 41 seconds for the whole instrument, and the respondent chose the first acceptable option in every grid and the same answer in all 14 attitude items. The stated median completion time for that instrument is 11 minutes. Which reading fits?

options.text: The respondent stopped at the first option that let them finish, so the record satisfies the questionnaire's form and carries little information about what they think
The respondent answered efficiently, so a short completion time is a sign of an experienced panelist rather than of a low-quality record

options.misconception: justifies a uniform response as sensible behaviour on a homogeneous topic

options.text: The record is anomalous and must be excluded outright, since no interview can legitimately be completed in that time
options.misconception: proposes an automatic exclusion rule that would remove hurried genuine answers too

options.misconception: reads consistency between items as evidence of the construct being measured

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: An order effect and the design that controls it
questions.learningObjective: identify order effects and the design that removes them
questions.stem: When the satisfaction items were asked before the complaints item, 44 per cent reported a complaint; when the complaints item came first, 61 per cent did. Which statement is the correct diagnosis?

options.text: The position of the first item sets the frame the second is read in, so the difference is a property of the instrument's order rather than of either question
The first version produced more complaints, because asking about complaints first makes a respondent more willing to report them at all
options.misconception: attributes the difference to a lasting change in the respondent rather than to position

options.text: The two versions measured different things, because a question means something different depending on what came before it in the same interview
options.misconception: states the mechanism as if it invalidated the question

options.text: The difference is sampling error, because two independent samples cannot agree to within a percentage point or two on a satisfaction measure
options.misconception: rejects a difference that is systematic and reproducible across versions

questions.explanation: An order effect is a dependence on what the respondent has already been asked, and the cleanest demonstration of it is exactly the one here: the same two items, the same sample, two orders, a difference of seventeen points. The mechanism is that the first item establishes what the interview is about, so a complaint asked after a run of praise is read as a qualification of something already praised while the same question asked first is read as a description of the service. A randomised or rotated order fixes the general problem, but it does not fix this one, because a randomisation still leaves roughly half the sample with the frame in place, so an order-sensitive pair of items has to be split deliberately between two versions, and the analysis has to acknowledge which version a respondent saw. questions.topic: Fatigue in the closing items of a long form

The later pages are harder to read, because a rising missing rate with page number indicates a difficulty gradient across the form
options.misconception: explains a rising rate as difficulty rather than as the length of the task

options.text: The middle category is the most popular answer on any grid, so the concentration at the end is the normal shape of a rating scale
options.misconception: generalises from the finding rather than explaining why it appears only at the end

options.text: The last grid should be removed, because an instrument that tires its respondents has failed whatever the earlier pages showed
options.misconception: jumps from a diagnosis to discarding a section rather than to a remedy

questions.topic: A missing-data pattern and what it licenses
questions.learningObjective: classify a missing-data mechanism from its pattern
questions.stem: In a follow-up survey, the pre-treatment wellbeing score is missing for 4 per cent of participants who completed the follow-up, and for 29 per cent of those who did not. Which classification fits?

The score is missing at random, because the amount of missingness cannot exceed the amount not collected at follow-up
options.misconception: defines the mechanism from the size of the missingness rather than its cause

options.text: The score is missing at random, because the proportion missing is a property of the instrument and not of who was measured
options.misconception: attributes missingness to the instrument when it varies with the outcome

options.text: The score is missing completely at random, since the two percentages are different and a pattern rules out any randomness at all
options.misconception: equates a pattern with a violation of randomness rather than with a dependence

The skip logic failed for the whole sample, so the routing rule needs to be removed and every question shown to everyone

options.misconception: proposes removing the skip rather than fixing the mismatch

options.text: The affected records should be dropped, because a respondent who answers a question they cannot answer has misunderstood the whole form
options.misconception: discards whole records over a localised routing defect

questions.learningObjective: identify the check a vignette requires before its answers are used

options.misconception: turns a survey instrument into a group method on the strength of one concern

options.misconception: asserts a direction the two percentages do not show

questions.topic: A representativeness claim the frame contradicts
questions.learningObjective: identify the frame defect behind a representativeness claim
questions.stem: A survey of graduates' earnings reports that its sample is representative of all graduates, and its frame is the membership file of two professional bodies whose membership requires an annual fee and excludes anyone who has left the profession. The sample is representative, because membership of a professional body is a close proxy for having graduated from any institution

options.misconception: believes a large response rate repairs a frame that excludes a group outright

options.text: The claim is a matter for the funder, since no survey can claim representativeness of a population defined after the fieldwork
options.misconception: reassigns a definitional problem to the body's sponsor

questions.topic: An item-wording experiment and the effect it estimates
questions.learningObjective: state what a wording experiment can establish
questions.stem: A team suspects that the word should in an item changes answers. First say what the experiment must do for its estimate to be interpretable, then say what the resulting difference establishes.

options.text: Randomly split the sample between the two wordings and hold everything else fixed, and the resulting difference in the response distributions is an estimate of the effect of that word in that context
Ask both wordings of the same respondents and compare, and the difference measures how much the wording matters to a particular person
options.misconception: uses a within-person design and reports a between-person effect

options.text: Change the wording in the next wave and compare that wave with the previous one, and the difference shows how much the word moved opinion
options.misconception: attributes a wave-to-wave difference to a word and ignores everything else that moved

options.text: Show the two wordings to a small expert panel and ask which is better, and the panel's preference estimates the size of the wording effect on answers
options.misconception: substitutes an expert judgement for a measured difference in responses

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A latent construct and the problem of its indicators
questions.learningObjective: explain why one item cannot stand for a construct
questions.stem: A construct such as trust in an institution is not directly observed, so a scale is built from items each standing in for it. Explain why the number of items matters, and what a single item leaves unestablished.

answer.exemplar: A construct is a pattern of behaviour and belief that produces several different observations, and no one of those observations is the construct itself, so a scale works by treating the items as indicators whose agreement is evidence that something common to them is doing the work. One item gives no such evidence, because a single response is equally consistent with the respondent's standing on the construct and with a passing mood, a particular recent event, a reading of that particular sentence, or a desire to give a particular answer, and nothing in the data distinguishes between those. Several items that behave as though they share a cause, varying together more than they vary with unrelated content, turn that ambiguity into an inference about a latent quantity, and they also make it possible to see which item is not behaving, since a single misworded item shows up as the one that correlates weakly while the rest hold. The remaining cost is that a scale is a decision, not a discovery: the choice of which indicators to use, how they are worded and how many, fixes the construct as much as measures it, so a report has to give the items, the response format and the evidence that the indicators hang together, rather than reporting a score and calling it the trait. A single item, by contrast, produces a number with no error estimate of its own and no way to find out whether it means what the analysis assumes.

questions.explanation: A strong response explains that indicators agree because a common cause is doing the work, that a single item cannot distinguish a stable trait from a passing circumstance or a reading of that sentence, and that a multi-item scale makes the misfit of any one item visible.
questions.hint: Ask what a single response is equally consistent with besides a standing on the construct.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Why a quota sample resists design-based standard errors
questions.learningObjective: explain the inference that a quota sample cannot support
questions.stem: A quota sample fixes the number of interviews in each cell of a table of characteristics. Explain why the usual formula-based standard errors and design-based tests cannot be applied to it as they are to a probability sample.

answer.exemplar: Those formulas derive their variance from the selection process, from the fact that each unit had a known probability of entering the sample and that the analysis can therefore reconstruct the sampling variability of the estimate. A quota sample fixes cell totals and leaves the choice of individuals to a recruiter, so no unit has a known selection probability, there is no frame-level probability of the realised configuration to condition on, and the errors are correlated because the same person made the choices, which means the variance of a quota estimate is not recoverable from the sample's own composition. Two practical consequences follow. First, a narrow interval around a quota estimate is a statement about nothing, because there is no sampling variance to bound it, and quoting one invites the reader to treat a recruitment artefact as precision. Second, a significance test comparing groups within a quota sample is testing a difference that was partly designed in, since the cell totals are set in advance, so a difference between cells is a property of the quota table and a difference within a cell is a property of the recruitment and neither is a finding about the population without an assumption the design cannot supply. The honest response is to report the achieved composition, state that the design is non-probability, and either limit the claims to description or anchor them with a small probability sample used for weighting and for the variance estimate.

questions.explanation: A strong response ties standard errors to a known selection probability, notes that a quota sample has none and that the recruiter's choices are correlated, and concludes that intervals and tests applied to it are not interpretable.
questions.hint: Ask what the variance of a quota estimate is calculated from, and whether a quota supplies that.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Why nonresponse weighting needs a measured auxiliary
questions.learningObjective: explain the limits of a nonresponse adjustment
questions.stem: Respondents and nonrespondents are compared on age, region, education and employment, and the responders are reweighted to the frame's distribution on those four. Explain what the adjustment can and cannot repair, and why the four variables were chosen.

answer.exemplar: A nonresponse adjustment works by making the responding group look like the frame on the variables used for the adjustment, and it is exactly as strong as the relationship between those variables and the missingness. The four were chosen because they are available in the frame for the respondents and for the nonrespondents, so a comparison is possible, and because they are plausibly related both to who responds and to the outcome being measured, which is what makes the reweighting informative rather than cosmetic. What it cannot repair is any part of the difference that runs through a variable the adjustment does not use, and the usual culprit is the outcome itself: people who have experienced the thing being asked about are more likely both to answer and to answer strongly, so a weighted estimate remains biased towards engagement even when it matches the frame perfectly on all four variables. That is why an adjustment is reported with the assumption it rests on, and why the useful companion is a direct comparison of responders with a subsample of nonrespondents, which is the only way to estimate how much of the difference the four variables account for. Making the responders match the frame on age, region, education and employment is a claim that what is left over is random, and the reader is entitled to know whether that claim was tested or merely asserted.

questions.explanation: A strong response states that the adjustment only removes the part of the nonresponse difference carried by the variables used, names the unmeasured outcome-related difference that remains, and distinguishes an adjustment from a test of it.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Why frame coverage cannot be weighted away
questions.learningObjective: explain why a coverage defect is not repairable by reweighting
questions.stem: A survey's frame omits a group entirely, and the team proposes to correct it by giving every sampled record a weight. Explain why that proposal cannot work, and what the estimate it produces actually describes.

answer.exemplar: A weight is a multiplier applied to records that exist, so it can rebalance a group that was sampled too often or too little often, and it does this by changing how much each held record counts relative to the others. It cannot do anything at all for a group that produced no records, because there is no record to multiply, and no quantity of arithmetic recovers a distribution over people who were never in the sampling units. The consequence is not a small residual bias but a change in what the estimate is about: the weights can make the respondents match the frame on everything the frame records, and the result is a well-calibrated estimate of the population as the frame defines it, which excludes the omitted group entirely. This is why the two coverage failures are not variants of one problem. Undercoverage removes units, and no reweighting reinstates them, whereas a frame that includes units which do not belong can be corrected, because the ineligible cases are present and can be removed or downweighted. The only repairs for undercoverage are at the design stage, a supplementary source for the omitted group combined into the frame, or an explicit statement of the population the estimate covers, so that a reader is not invited to read a frame-limited figure as a population figure.

questions.explanation: A strong response notes that a weight acts only on records that exist, concludes that the estimate covers the frame's population rather than the target population, and separates undercoverage from a frame containing ineligible units.
questions.hint: Ask what a weight does to a group that produced no records at all.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Translation equivalence is not measurement equivalence
questions.learningObjective: distinguish linguistic equivalence from measurement equivalence
questions.stem: A back-translation of every item comes back close to the English original. Explain why the two languages can still differ in what the scale measures, and what would have to be tested to know.

answer.exemplar: A back-translation is a check on the words, and the words are one link in a longer chain. The scale is used to rank people on a construct, and a construct has a scale of its own that differs between languages, since the words a respondent uses for an everyday state are not spread across the range in the same way in two languages, and a category that sits in the middle of one distribution can sit at one end of the other. It follows that a respondent who has picked the same ordinal position on a translated item may be at a different point on the construct, and a scale that is internally consistent within each language can therefore be measuring two different things, which is a statement about measurement rather than about translation and which no back-translation can detect because the two versions can be faithful translations of words that carry different scales. What would have to be tested is invariance: whether the pattern of how items relate to one another, and whether the meaning of each response position, can be held constant across the two language groups, and that requires a sample in each language with enough cases for the comparison to mean anything. A translation described as equivalent and a scale described as comparable are two different claims, and a report should make them separately.

questions.explanation: A strong response separates a check on the words from a check on the construct, notes that two language versions can be faithful yet place a response position differently on the underlying scale, and identifies invariance testing as the check that would settle it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the same words and the same construct can be guaranteed to be the same thing in two languages.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Why a screener's wording changes who is recruited
questions.learningObjective: explain how screener wording shapes the recruited sample
questions.stem: Two versions of a screener ask for the same thing, one as have you been unemployed for more than six months and one as are you currently out of work and looking for work. Explain why the recruited groups can differ even though the criteria are meant to be identical.

answer.exemplar: A screener does not select a group, it defines one, and the definition reaches the recruit through the words. Unemployment in the sense of the benefit or the labour-market statistic is an administrative status with a precise start date, while being out of work and looking is a description of a situation that a person may recognise in themselves and may also recognise in a way the statistic does not capture: a person who has stopped registering because they believe no work is available, or who is doing a few hours of casual work, or who has left a job to retrain, may answer yes to the second and be counted in the first, and may answer the first with a date they have to look up and then decline the interview rather than answer inaccurately. Each wording therefore produces a different pass rate and a different membership, and since the screener's result becomes part of the analysis rather than a preliminary, the choice is a design decision that determines the population the results describe. The practical requirements follow: pre-test the exact wording, report the wording verbatim in the methods, report the achieved pass rate, and treat the recruited group as a defined population whose characteristics may differ from the administrative count it is named after.

questions.explanation: A strong response treats the screener as a definition rather than a filter, explains how a lay and an administrative description capture different people, and derives the requirements to pre-test and report the exact wording.
questions.hint: Ask what a person recognises as belonging to, and whether that is the same group the criterion names.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Building a questionnaire in the right order
questions.learningObjective: sequence the decisions that precede a finished instrument
questions.stem: A team is about to write a questionnaire and has not decided anything yet. Put these steps in the order they should be carried out.

options.text: Write down the constructs to be measured and the decisions about each that the analysis will need
Decide how each construct will be observed, and whether the proposed items can in fact be answered by a respondent
Draft the items and put them in a matrix so that the response options are the same wherever the same construct appears
Choose the order, the length and the mode, and place the qualifying questions and the checks in their positions
Pre-test the draft and revise it, treating every change as a decision to be recorded rather than a preference

questions.explanation: The constructs come first because every later decision is a decision about how one of them will be observed, and a team that starts with items has already made those decisions implicitly and cannot revise them without discarding the work. Observability comes next, since a construct with no observable consequence produces items nobody can answer consistently, and discovering that after drafting is the most expensive place to discover it. Drafting into a matrix rather than a list is what makes the response options comparable across items of one construct, which is a precondition for the internal consistency a scale is supposed to show, and it also exposes the double-barrelled item before it reaches a respondent. The order, length and mode are decided after the items exist, because a form's length is a consequence of how many decisions it contains rather than a target to be hit, and the qualifying questions and the checks are placed last, when their positions can be chosen against the finished form. Pre-testing then tests the instrument rather than the intentions behind it.
questions.hint: Ask which decision constrains all the others, and which step tests what the earlier steps assumed.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Turning a construct into a usable set of items
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps from a construct to an item set
questions.stem: A researcher has chosen a construct and must produce the items that will stand for it. Put these steps in the order they should be carried out.

options.text: Write a definition of the construct, including what a high score and a low score would each mean in practice
Generate a larger pool of candidate statements, including items worded in both directions
Judge the pool against criteria for specificity, simplicity and whether a respondent could plausibly know the answer
Pre-test the surviving items in a cognitive interview and a pilot, and drop the ones that do not behave as indicators
Fix the number of items, the response format and the scoring rule, and record them before the scale is used in an analysis

questions.explanation: The definition comes first because an item is a question about a specified meaning, and a team that generates items before agreeing what the construct means produces a pool that samples several related constructs and discovers the disagreement only when the items fail to agree with one another. The pool is then generated wide, because the cost of an item that later fails is small and the cost of having none for a facet of the construct is a scale that does not cover it, and generating in both directions is what allows an acquiescence tendency to be examined rather than assumed absent. Judging the pool against criteria is what turns a brainstorm into a set, and each criterion removes a different kind of failure: a double-barrelled item, an item in an idiom, an item asking for an opinion the respondent has not formed. Pre-testing then establishes which survivors behave as indicators rather than as questions about wording, and the count, the response format and the scoring rule are fixed at the end so that the scale cannot be quietly reshaped once results are in view.
questions.hint: Ask what the items are questions about, and which step establishes that they answer it.
