questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Handling a suspected data-quality problem in returned data
questions.learningObjective: sequence the response to a suspected data-quality problem
questions.stem: A fieldwork team spots a pattern in the returned records that looks like a routing failure. Put these steps in the order they should be carried out.

options.text: Quantify the pattern: how many records it affects, and whether it concentrates in particular segments of the sample
Check the form specification to see whether the page and the jump carry the same condition on display
Identify the affected records individually, using a rule that does not depend on the answers the defect corrupted
Recompute the results with those records excluded, and compare them with the results as they stand
Report the defect, the rule, the counts and the comparison, so a reader can see what was done and whether it mattered

questions.explanation: Quantifying comes first because a pattern that affects two records in ten thousand is a footnote and the same pattern affecting a fifth of the sample changes the study, and the quantification also reveals whether the defect is spread evenly or concentrated, which is itself evidence about its cause. Checking the specification follows, since a routing defect is either an implementation error or a specification error and the two have different fixes, and the specification is the document that settles it. The affected records are then identified individually and by a rule that avoids the corrupted answers, since a rule defined in terms of the field the defect overwrote will select the wrong records or none. Only then is the analysis rerun, because the comparison is what converts a suspected problem into a known cost, and the whole sequence is reported, because a defect that was detected and fixed but not disclosed leaves a reader unable to tell whether the fix was complete.
questions.hint: Ask how many records the pattern touches, and then what a reader must be shown about them.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Choosing and documenting a data collection mode
questions.learningObjective: sequence the decisions that precede a mode being fixed
questions.stem: A survey has to fix how the interviews will be conducted before the field period starts. Put these steps in the order they should be carried out.

options.text: Establish which parts of the target population each candidate mode can and cannot reach
Compare the cost per completed case across the modes, remembering that nonresponse raises the cost of the expensive modes fastest
Check whether the questionnaire can be delivered in the chosen mode without changing what the questions ask
Establish the fieldwork and quality controls the chosen mode requires, and what they can detect
Record the choice, the rejected alternatives and the reasons, so a later reader can see what the mode excludes

questions.explanation: Coverage comes first because the mode is a selection condition, and a decision about cost made before the reach of each option is known optimises the wrong quantity, since the cheap mode that misses a third of the population is not cheaper in any sense the study cares about. The cost comparison comes second and is not the same calculation as a list of prices, because a mode that needs several visits per complete is priced per visit and its effective price rises with the nonresponse rate, which is highest for the modes that are already the most expensive. Whether the questionnaire survives the mode is third, since a question that needs a diagram or a long written scenario cannot be put to a telephone respondent without changing it, and a mode change that alters the instrument changes the measurement. The controls follow, because each mode has its own failure modes and its own detectable signatures, and the record comes last so that the choice and its exclusions are inspectable.
questions.hint: Ask which option reaches whom, and what the record has to say about the options not chosen.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A completion-time distribution read as evidence
questions.learningObjective: interpret a table of completion times against the data-quality rule
questions.stem: A web instrument has a median completion time of 640 seconds. Its 400 returns divide as follows: 28 cases at or below 90 seconds, 61 cases between 90 and 180 seconds, 244 cases above 180 seconds, and 67 cases that the platform logged as zero because the tab was closed. What is the fair reading?

options.text: A distinct fast group sits well below the bulk of the returns, so a rule at 90 seconds flags 7 per cent of cases, and the zero group has to be resolved rather than treated as very fast
The distribution is continuous, so any cut-point chosen would be arbitrary and the safest course is to keep every case in the analysis
options.misconception: reads a separated group as part of one smooth distribution

options.text: The 67 zero-second cases are impossible, so the platform's logging is broken and the whole timing field is unusable
options.misconception: discards a whole field on the strength of one class of value

options.text: The fast cases are genuine, because 28 cases at or below 90 seconds is a small enough share to be treated as ordinary variation
options.misconception: treats a small share as immaterial regardless of how it differs

questions.explanation: The counts describe a distribution with a separated group rather than a single spread: 244 cases sit above 180 seconds, 61 lie between 90 and 180, and 28 lie at or below 90, so a threshold at 90 seconds separates 7 per cent of the returns from the rest on the face of the numbers rather than by judgment. That is the shape a satisficing group makes, and the rule is defensible precisely because it sits in a gap, which is also why the choice of cut-point should be shown rather than asserted. The 67 zero-second cases are a separate problem of a different kind, since a zero is a logging outcome and not a duration, and it has to be resolved, by another field or by excluding those records and saying so, because silently treating them as the fastest returns would let a platform artefact inflate the very flag being examined. Options B, C and D each either smooth away the separation, discard the field, or excuse the group.
questions.hint: Ask whether the fast cases are separated from the bulk or merely part of it, and what a duration of zero is reporting.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A field table of response rates read against the frame
questions.learningObjective: interpret a table of response rates by subgroup
questions.stem: A survey of 4,000 sampled adults reports completes by group as 61 per cent of the 1,200 sampled aged 18 to 29, 44 per cent of the 1,900 aged 30 to 59, and 22 per cent of the 900 aged 60 and over. The report states the estimate covers adults. What is the fair reading?

options.text: The completion rate falls steeply with age, so the respondents are younger than the frame and any unweighted estimate understates older adults' answers unless it is adjusted for that
The overall completion rate is the one that matters, so the group differences are a normal feature of fieldwork and need no comment
options.misconception: treats an average as sufficient and the pattern beneath it as noise

options.text: Older adults are less willing to be surveyed, so the low rate reflects a stable attitude that no adjustment should correct
options.misconception: reads a response propensity as a substantive opinion about being surveyed

options.text: The estimate is unusable, because a design that produces different rates across age groups cannot produce an estimate for adults at all
options.misconception: condemns the whole design over a correctable imbalance

questions.explanation: The three rates are the whole content of the table, and they fall monotonically and steeply with age, so the responding group is systematically younger than the sampled group and the size of the departure is quantifiable from the table: with 732, 836 and 198 completes against 1,200, 1,900 and 900 sampled, the age composition of the returns differs visibly from the frame's. Because nonresponse is associated with a variable the study also measures, this is a bias and not only a loss of precision, and the standard response is to weight the returns to the frame's distribution on age, with the caveat that any weighting can only correct on the variables used and cannot reach a difference the adjustment does not carry. Options B and C each dismiss a pattern that the table states plainly, and option D treats a correctable imbalance as fatal.
questions.hint: Ask whether the age composition of the returns matches the age composition of the sample.
